title: “Ideas Are Worth Scrap”: How Zorko Built 550+ Outlets and Rs 200 Cr GMV With a No-Chef, No-Royalty Franchise Model
excerpt: In a viral episode of Season 3 of Shark Tank India, Aman Gupta made Anand and Amrit Nahar an offer, then tore up the cheque. The brothers from Surat had walked in asking Rs 1.5 crore for one percent equity. The sharks came back with a mix of equity and debt, and the negotiation unravelled as the brothers pressed for committed advisory time. Gupta’s reservations grew as the brothers insisted on specific advisory hours, which he was unwilling to commit to. The negotiations became one of the most viral moments of Shark Tank India. In an exclusive interview with Startup Pedia, Anand Nahar, co-founder of Zorko, a pure vegetarian fast-food franchise chain in India, shares that when he and Aman Gupta recently crossed paths again, two years after the show aired, they were both guest lecturers at IIT BHU. Gupta greeted him with a wistful line, “Hojani chahiye thi humari deal (Our deal should have materialised).” Today, Zorko says it runs more than 500 outlets in more than 275 cities. It is an interesting reversal for a company that began in 2020, not as a restaurant brand but as a seller of Rs 30 immunity-booster sachets. How Zorko began The Nahar brothers, Anand and Amrit, were both engineers by profession. The brothers grew up in a shopkeeper’s household: their father ran an electrical appliance store. Amrit Nahar pursued a BE in Environmental Engineering. Anand, on the other hand, pursued a BTech in Automobile Engineering from Uka Tarsadia University. While pursuing his BTech, Anand worked as a SEBI-registered research analyst covering the stock markets from 2017 to 2020. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, they ventured into entrepreneurship. The first startup they built sold immunity boosters during the pandemic, when vaccines had not yet been developed. “The Ministry of Ayush, which is responsible for traditional and alternative healthcare systems in India, had suggested that people use traditional herbal remedies to strengthen their immune system. But these Kaadhas would often irritate the body. We built a herbal concoction with 14 herbs which weren’t harsh on the body,” says Anand. They named their business “Zorko Immunity Boosters”. The same year they trademarked the name. “Zorko is a Marwari slang which means powerful, tremendous, excellent, or amazing. When we’d discuss naming our business, my mother would say, “Zorko kaam karjo/Do everything with full power”. We decided to name our brand Zorko as it was unique and easily trademarkable,” he shares. A 26-year-old at the time, Anand says they invested Rs 50,000 in their immunity booster business. They sold a packet of their booster sachets for Rs 30, which could be used for a week. “We used Whatsapp and Facebook groups to market it. People found it affordable and in the absence of an alternative, they found it useful. A lot of people reached out to us for distribution as well,” he adds. They earned over Rs 60 lakh in revenue between 2020 and 2021. When Covid vaccines were rolled out, the duo slowed down their business and gradually pivoted in a different direction. Pivoting towards food “During the pandemic, cooking became a popular hobby in our household. We realised that food which we would otherwise be able to buy at expensive prices from restaurants could be made at home at minimal costs. This got us thinking and we decided to explore the idea of starting a food business,” Anand says. In 2021, due to the pandemic, a lot of businesses were shutting down. The brothers chanced upon an outlet in Vesu, in the southwestern part of Surat, where a shop was being sold for Rs 4.5 lakh. “In India, places selling good food are often expensive. Outlets which sell cheap food often compromise on quality. In rare cases when one does find good quality food at affordable prices, the ambience is not great. We wanted to open an outlet which had all three: quality, affordability, and ambience,” Nahar explains. For vegetarians, one-stop fast food barely existed. Pizza in one place, burgers in another, fries and mojitos somewhere else. Zorko set out to put it all on one menu. From idea to execution Anand has little patience for the romance of the big idea. “An idea has no value. In the age of AI, an idea is not even worth kabad,” he says, using the Hindi word for scrap. “Execution is everything.” Initially, logistics turned out to be a big issue. Every outlet depended on a steady flow of premixes, sauces and raw materials from the company, and serving those far from Surat proved far more expensive than the founders had planned for. “It was very difficult to cater to, say, one far-off outlet in Chhattisgarh,” Anand says. “Serving even one was very expensive.” At one stage, logistics cost the company more than the raw materials it was shipping. Packaging had to be redesigned, and a detail the team had dismissed, the “handle with care” label, turned out to matter. “In the beginning, we didn’t know any of this,” Anand says. “We found out later.” Eventually, instead of booking dedicated vehicles, Zorko began sending goods with buses and trucks already running on a given route. “If we found a bus or a truck going on a particular route, we’d work with it,” he says. “It turned out to be cheaper for us.” For Zorko, he says, the hardest part of execution was scale. The brothers had grown up with a different model of business. “Our family business was traditional. You have a small team, a shop, and you do all the work yourself,” Anand says. “In the business we were trying to run, we realised much later that one needs a great team as well.” That realisation shaped how Zorko treats its people. A good team, Anand argues, can only be built through better working conditions and fair compensation. He also attributes Zorko’s initial growth to word-of-mouth recommendations. “India loves sharing,” Anand says, “especially when it comes to where people have eaten well. That’s what has worked for us.” Within 17 months of its launch, Zorko had opened 150 outlets across six states, the majority of them in Gujarat. Reflections on the Shark Tank experience Asked what he considers the most significant moment in Zorko’s journey, Anand points to their participation in Season 3 of Shark Tank India, though not necessarily for the pitch or the deal itself. What made the difference, he says, was how the company prepared to make the most of the exposure. “More than the exposure we got through Shark Tank, we benefited because of the preparations we had done to handle the inquiries that came after the episode aired,” he says. “We were able to capitalise on that exposure.” The preparations began even before the brothers knew whether their segment would make the final cut. “One doesn’t know for certain if your part will be part of the show or not. You only find out three or four days before,” Anand says. Rather than wait for confirmation, the brothers decided to prepare anyway. They worked on their presentation, approached the opportunity with confidence, and kept in mind that the show needed engaging content to draw viewers. They also made a calculated bet on the potential response. Zorko rented a large office and assembled a team of 15 to 20 people dedicated exclusively to handling Shark Tank-related inquiries. The team was trained to answer frequently asked questions and respond to callers as soon as the episode aired, with the aim of converting inquiries into leads. The move came with a financial risk. Had the segment not aired, the company would still have been responsible for paying the team’s salaries for two months. “We took that risk,” Anand says. The uncertainty was difficult for the team. “Our team would keep asking when the real calls would start. We just kept them patient,” he recalls. Once the episode aired, however, the calls began, and the team was ready. “We catered to all inquiries. We left no platform unattended.” The strategy paid off. “Shark Tank made people trust our brand and helped it grow. People were willing to pay us the booking amount for the franchise without even visiting us,” Anand says. After the show, he continued building on the momentum through multiple podcast appearances and guest lectures, using each opportunity to bring further attention to Zorko. Zorko now Anand says Zorko runs more than 550 outlets across 275 cities in 25 states today. Zorko’s growth owes much to its business model. Anand says Zorko charges its outlets no royalty. Franchise fees account for about 25% of its revenue, while the remaining 75% comes from the raw materials it supplies to these outlets: sauces, syrups, premixes and masalas. “The company runs on a chefless kitchen model, which means anyone can operate an outlet. Zorko provides the recipes and the ingredients, and its standard operating procedures are simple enough that a large kitchen team is not required,” he explains. The structure, Anand says, ties the company’s fortunes to its outlets. Because Zorko earns most of its revenue by supplying them, an outlet reorders only if its business is doing well. “When they win, we win,” he says. “We depend on each other’s success, and that is how we keep the business healthy.” Zorko’s support to outlet owners goes beyond supplies. The company provides the raw materials, the concept, menu development and ongoing operational help, which means newcomers can enter the business without any background in food. “Even a person who knows nothing about food can start at Zorko and set up a business,” Anand says. The company has also expanded its portfolio with two additional brands: Cheese Corner, which operates more than 75 outlets, and UK Waffle, which has over 50. Chaat Ka Baap is slated to follow. Across its network, Zorko records system-wide sales of Rs 17 to 18 crore a month and closed last year with GMV of Rs 200 crore. The company’s own revenue, earned from raw-material supplies and franchise fees, stood at Rs 46 crore. Beyond numbers, the founder says that recognition has mattered more. In 2024, Nahar brothers made it to the Forbes 30 Under 30 Asia list, a moment he describes as deeply reassuring. Anand Nahar’s advice to all founders is simpler than any pitch. “Do not merely sit on an idea. You can figure things out as you go. Start now,” he concludes. FAQ Q. Who founded Zorko? A. Zorko was founded by brothers Anand Nahar and Amrit Nahar, who started their entrepreneurial journey in Surat in 2020. How did Zorko start its business? The brothers initially launched an immunity booster made with 14 herbs in 2020. They invested Rs 50,000, sold sachets for Rs 30 each and generated over Rs 60 lakh in revenue between 2020 and 2021. They later pivoted to the food business. What happened to Zorko on Shark Tank India? The brothers appeared on Season 3 of Shark Tank India, seeking Rs 1.5 crore for one percent equity. Negotiations broke down over the advisory hours they wanted from the investors. Aman Gupta eventually tore up the cheque and withdrew his offer. How does Zorko's franchise model work? Zorko follows a chefless kitchen model and charges franchisees no royalty. It provides recipes, ingredients, premixes, sauces, menu development and operational support. Franchise fees account for around 25% of its revenue, while raw-material supplies contribute the remaining 75%. How much revenue does Zorko generate, and how many outlets does it have? Zorko says it operates more than 550 outlets across 275 cities in 25 states. Its network records monthly system-wide sales of Rs 17-18 crore. The company closed last year with Rs 200 crore in GMV and Rs 46 crore in revenue.
